justification_text:
My point estimates for all horizons—one day, one week, and one month—converged on 944.97. This consistent figure represents my central expectation for the value at each future point in time. It is likely anchored to the most recent observed data point or a well-established current trend. In the absence of strong, immediate directional indicators, this value is considered the most probable outcome. It acts as the baseline around which future fluctuations are expected to occur, reflecting an assumption that current conditions or a recent average will largely persist, even as the range of possible outcomes widens over time.

The widening of the confidence intervals, from a relatively narrow band for the one-day forecast to a much broader range for the one-month forecast, directly reflects the escalating uncertainty associated with longer time horizons. For the one-day forecast, uncertainty is primarily driven by immediate market dynamics, minor news, or typical daily fluctuations. As we extend to one week, and especially to one month, a multitude of factors contribute to greater unpredictability. These include the potential for new economic data releases, shifts in monetary policy, unforeseen geopolitical developments, company-specific news or industry trends (depending on what the number represents), and broader market sentiment changes. Each of these elements introduces additional variability, making it harder to pinpoint the exact future value, thus requiring a wider interval to capture 90% of the probable outcomes.

While the confidence intervals aim to capture 90% of outcomes under normal market conditions and typical volatility, certain significant risks or "black swan" events could push actual results beyond these boundaries. These are typically low-probability, high-impact occurrences that are difficult to model within standard forecasting frameworks. Examples include a sudden and severe global economic recession or an unexpected boom, the outbreak or escalation of a major geopolitical conflict, a widespread natural disaster or pandemic with significant economic repercussions, or a disruptive technological breakthrough or failure that fundamentally alters an industry. Such unforeseen events could introduce extreme volatility and create outcomes that fall outside the 90% confidence bands, necessitating a reassessment of fundamental assumptions.
